column3: Introduces fundamental programming concepts such as data types, control structures, functions, and arrays using a high-level language (Python).

This course covers the fundamental concepts and techniques of data analysis. It introduces students to data modeling, extraction, preprocessing, transformation, plotting, and visualization. Students will be introduced to Python, NumPy and Pandas.
Focuses on programming applications for engineering problems, covering numerical methods, simulation, and algorithmic thinking in python
Provides an overview of computer systems, software, and hardware components, introducing students to the basics of algorithmmic problem solving and programming logic.

This course will build on the knowledge and skills acquired in the introductory programming course. It covers different types of data structures (lists, queues, graphs, etc.) and the associated algorithms, emphasizing memory vs. CPU tradeoffs

This course will allow students to scale-up and solve problems using objected-oriented methodology. . Students will gain experience building object-oriented
software solutions using the Unified Modeling Language (UML) and the Java programming language.

This course provides a discussion of the fundamentals of computer organization and architecture and relates it to contemporary design issues.Topics include digital logic, instruction set architecture, computer
arithmetic, architectural CPU design, and functional computer organization.

This course examines computer languages from the perspective of translation and the computational models they implement. The first half of the course reviews the evolution of languages, language design principles, and evaluation criteria, then presents the processing stages, theoretical concepts, and tools associated with language translation. The second half of the course introduces languages representing different programming paradigms and examines runtime handling of selected language features.

This course covers the study of algorithm design, including introductory concepts: sorting and searching algorithms; string, graph, and set algorithms; complexity classes; branch and bound algorithms; dynamic programming, and advanced topics.

Software Engineering is the application of engineering principles and techniques to the process of software development, delivery, maintenance, and decommission. Its purpose is to make the building of software systems formal and predictable, while delivering high quality software products that comply with client requirements and expectations.

This course introduces students to fundamental concepts of operating systems. It emphasizes structures, key design issues, as well as the fundamental principles behind modern operating systems. It covers concurrency, scheduling, memory and device management, file systems, and scripting. The course uses implementations of Unix-like and Windows systems to illustrate some concepts.

The course covers the design and implementation of Relational databases. While significant focus is placed on Entity-Relationship and Relational modeling, other models and current trends in database are introduced. Relational Algebra and SQL are covered, including procedural SQL. A Relational DBMS is used along with database application development as lab work and class projects.

This course provides theoretical knowledge about, and practical skills in advanced programming paradigms. It builds on the background acquired in introductory programming courses and other prerequisite courses to tackle programming models used in professional, enterprise-grade software development.

This course covers topics in data communications of interest to computing majors, such as types of LAN,
VLAN, MAN, and WAN networks, with their corresponding access methods and link layer protocols. The
course then moves on to cover the TCP/IP protocol stack, including IP functions such as addressing,
routing, congestion control, and Transport layer function, such as reliable transmission and flow control.

The course provides students with the concepts and knowledge to design intelligent agents by leveraging the main skills of AI programming, namely searching for goals and planning, knowledge representation, logical and probabilistic inferencing, data learning from experience.

This course introduces the students to the computing perspective of cybersecurity. It focuses on the role of cryptography in data and network security on the one hand and access control on the other. As such, the course covers the principles behind secret key encryption algorithms such as AES and message authentication functions (SHA-XXX, CMAC, HMAC), public key encryption (RSA, Diffie-Hellman, Elliptic curve cryptography), key management, and digital signatures.

This course surveys the application of computing systems in a range of devices ranging from nomadic devices to embedded real-time computers. Emphasis will be on developing applications for these platforms with stringent constraints such as low memory, limited power, limited processing power, no persistent storage capability, etc
Special topics in computer science. Courses may be taught by visiting or AUI faculty. This course is intended primarily for juniors and seniors. Can be repeated (not to exceed 6 SCH).

The course covers the most popular machine learning algorithms used for discovering meaningful patterns and knowledge from large amounts of data, including Artificial Neural Networks, Decision Trees, Association Rule Mining, Clustering algorithms, K-Nearest Neighbor approaches, etc.

This course defines biological, physical, and different mathematical models for Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), compares these models, and investigates the relationship between neural network learning and symbolic learning methods.

This course provides an introduction to computer vision including fundamentals of image formation, camera imaging geometry, feature detection and matching, stereo, motion estimation and tracking, image classification and scene understanding. The course will explore methods for depth recovery from stereo images, camera calibration, automated alignment, tracking, boundary detection, and recognition using both classical machine learning and deep learning approaches.
This course provides an introduction to the profession and practice of engineering.

column2: Natural Language Processing and Text Mining
column3: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the field of modeling and processing linguistic information. This field is extremely multidisciplinary; therefore, the course will include some ideas central to Linguistics (morphology, syntax, semantics), and to modeling (probabilistic models, machine learning models). In recent years, deep learning approaches have obtained very high performance in NLP. Hence, besides investigating the fundamental concepts, students will gain an introduction to the cutting-edge neural network algorithms that have revolutionized the world of NLP for avariety of tasks and have a high impact in industry.

column2: Introduction to Big Data Environment and Applications
column3: The course introduces Big Data management and techniques that can be applied to massive datasets in distributed environments. The course covers the Map-Reduce parallel computing paradigm and Hadoop distributed file system. The course reviews data storage and preparation for applications, including some machine learning algorithms used for mining knowledge in datastores, including NoSQL.

This course provides concepts and tools for building and adapting data-oriented analytical models based on massive data of different formats, using the parallel and distributed programming paradigms and data structures.

This course introduces students to the Internet of Things (IoT) world and technological trends. It covers IoT specific requirements and challenges, reference architecture, components and protocols, as well as state of the art IoT cloud platforms and architectural patterns. As IoT is a main source of big data, this course also addresses the cloud technologies and services necessary to support big data streaming and processing

This course covers two independent, but complementary parts, namely data engineering and data visualization. In the first part we will cover data engineering, which is a prerequisite to any data science/ analytics project. We will explore various ways in building and maintaining data architectures for ingestion and processing, as well as ways for ensuring that there is uninterrupted flow/pipeline of data between servers and analytics applications.The second part will cover the art and science of turning data into readable graphics. We will explore how
to design and create data visualizations based on data available and business objectives

The course covers some advanced issues in database systems, including database storage, indexing and query processing, etc. Significant focus is placed on data warehouse design and architecture, including the fundamental concepts of dimensional modeling, covering star schemas and OLAP cubes. ETL and analytical querying and reporting for better decision-support are addressed, using case study analysis and project design.
This course provides statistical methods and tools for analytics, helping students in applying them for purposes of data analysis, hypothesis testing, and building prediction and forecasting models.

The course focuses on the fundamentals of Cloud Computing technology and provides a broad understanding of the different enabling technologies, e.g., Virtualization and Distributed Systems. Topics include concepts and architecture, standards, implementation strategies, Software as a Service (SaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), software defined networks and storage, cloud storage, and programming models

This course teaches students how to build, debug, and test large computer programs. The course stresses learning how to use tools such as debuggers, profilers, source version control systems, and integrated development environments as an essential part of developing large programs. The course also stresses the understanding of how programs execute on today’s computers and how to measure and optimize performance

This course focuses on agility in software engineering: its values, principles, roles, practices, frameworks, and tools. It compares agile software development against traditional phase-based methodologies, such as Waterfall, to showcase the benefits of agility in modern software development

This course provides a solid background – both theoretical and practical – on the architecture, design and full stack development of enterprise-class, cloud-based, mobile-first progressive applications, based on well-defined security, performance, scalability, extensibility and integration requirements.

The purpose of this course is to take students through the process of object-oriented analysis and design using the Unified Modeling Language (UML) and the Unified Process (UP). This course introduces the rational unified process, then the fundamental principles of object-oriented approaches to modeling software requirements and design.

This course is intended to provide a theoretical background and hands-on knowledge of key elements for Blockchain for business applications developer. It introduces students to Blockchain concepts such as business networks, participants, assets, and trusted transactions, Hyperledger Fabric, Hyperledger Composer, and other Blockchain platforms, smart contracts, consensus, and architecture of Blockchain solutions.

The objective of this course is to emphasize the importance of testing, and to prepare students to test software in an organized and systematic way. This course will provide theoretical and practical knowledge, as well as current research on software testing. Upon completion of the course, students will be capable of planning and applying various testing techniques and strategies for testing software.
The course covers the principles, themes, processes and tools for project management, as well as their extension for agile project management.

This course is an introduction to the fundamental ideas of discrete mathematics. Topics covered in this course include logic, sets, relations, function, number representation, graphs, and counting techniques and their applications to probabilistic reasoning. The aim of the course is to give the students a foundation for the development of more advanced mathematical concepts that are used in computer science and engineering.
Multivariable calculus covers vectors and surfaces, partial differentiation, multiple integration, and vector calculus, including Green’s Theorem and Stokes’ Theorem.

The course covers differential equations, including basic concepts, first-order differential equations and applications, linear differential equations of higher order, series solutions, solutions using Laplace transforms, and solutions using numerical methods and applications.

Students are introduced to: vectors in R2 and R3, matrices and vectors; systems of linear equations, spanning sets, linear independence, linear transformations and matrix operators; LU decomposition of a matrix, determinants, subspaces, basis and dimension; coordinate systems and change of coordinates; eigenvalues and eigenvectors; orthogonality and orthogonal matrices; and applications of linear algebra to some computing and engineering problems.

This course is a calculus-based introduction to probability and statistics with a focus on techniques and applications most relevant to engineering. Topics include basic probability, conditional probability, independence of events, random variables, cumulative distribution functions, density functions, expectation, variance and covariance, independence of events and random variables, common discrete and continuous distributions, Law of Large Numbers, the Central Limit Theorem, and an introduction to descriptive statistics and sampling distributions
This course is a foundational course for freshmen students who do not meet the requirements of Calculus 1. It covers introductory concepts like functions, graphs, and differentiation.

This is an introductory mathematics course tailored for business administration students. It covers concepts related to linear and quadratic functions, simple and compound interest, and statistican and data analysis.

Examines the principles of international trade, foreign exchange markets, and global financial systems. Students explore trade policies, comparative advantage, and the economic relationships between nations.
Traces major global events and developments from World War I to contemporary times. The course examines world wars, decolonization, the Cold War, and the emergence of modern international relations.

Studies the legal frameworks governing relationships between nations, including treaties, international organizations, and dispute resolution mechanisms. Students explore topics like human rights law, trade agreements, and the laws of war.

Analyzes major theoretical frameworks used to understand global politics, including realism, liberalism, constructivism, and critical theories. Students examine how these perspectives explain conflict, cooperation, and power dynamics between states.

Compares different forms of government and political institutions across countries, examining democracies, authoritarian regimes, and hybrid systems. Students analyze how political structures, cultures, and historical contexts shape governance outcomes.

Explores how gender is represented, constructed, and challenged in various media forms including film, television, advertising, and digital platforms. Students critically analyze media''s role in shaping gender norms and identities.

Examines the relationship between gender identity, sexuality, and power structures in society. The course explores how gender hierarchies are maintained and contested across different social, political, and economic contexts.

Investigates women''s roles in economic systems and development processes globally. Students examine topics like women''s labor, entrepreneurship, poverty, and policies aimed at gender equity in economic participation.

Analyzes how gender shapes and is shaped by political institutions, social movements, and public policy. The course covers topics like women''s political participation, feminist movements, and gender-based policy issues.

Provides a comprehensive overview of human sexuality from biological, psychological, and sociocultural perspectives. Students explore topics including sexual identity, orientation, behavior, and contemporary issues in sexuality studies.
Offers focused examination of current issues, emerging research, or specialized themes in gender studies. Content varies by semester and instructor expertise.

Surveys the diverse histories of African societies south of the Sahara from precolonial times through the modern era. Students examine kingdoms, colonialism, independence movements, and contemporary developments.

Explores African cultural production including music, film, literature, fashion, and digital media. The course examines how popular culture reflects social change, identity, and Africa''s global connections.

Provides an overview of political systems, governance challenges, and democratic transitions in African countries. Students analyze topics like party systems, elections, civil society, and contemporary political issues.

Examines the geography, history, cultures, and contemporary issues of North African countries including Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco. The course explores the region''s distinct Arab-Berber identity and Mediterranean connections.
Surveys literary works by African authors across various genres and periods. Students explore how African writers address themes of colonialism, identity, tradition, modernity, and social change.

Analyzes Africa''s role in international relations, including its relationships with major powers, regional organizations, and global institutions. The course examines topics like peacekeeping, development aid, and Africa''s emerging global influence.
Investigates the causes, dynamics, and consequences of conflicts in modern Africa. Students examine civil wars, ethnic tensions, resource conflicts, and efforts toward peace and reconciliation.
Introduces ethnographic methods and anthropological perspectives on African societies. Students learn about fieldwork techniques and examine ethnographic studies of African communities and cultures.

Explores rapid urban growth in African cities, examining migration patterns, urban planning challenges, informal settlements, and the social and economic transformations of urban life. Students analyze the opportunities and problems created by Africa''s urbanization process.

column2: Political Economy of Development in Africa
column3: Examines the economic development trajectories of African nations, analyzing the intersection of political institutions and economic policies. The course covers topics like structural adjustment, natural resource management, foreign investment, and development strategies.

Studies the unique characteristics, historical development, and contemporary challenges of urban centers in North Africa. Students explore architecture, urban planning, social dynamics, and cultural heritage in cities like Cairo, Casablanca, and Tunis.
Provides in-depth examination of specific themes, regions, or issues in African studies. Course content varies to address current events, emerging scholarship, or specialized areas of inquiry.

Provides foundational knowledge of HRD principles, including employee training, career development, and organizational learning. Students explore how organizations invest in human capital to improve performance and achieve strategic goals.

column2: Business Environment and Ethics for HRD
column3: Examines ethical issues and decision-making frameworks relevant to human resource practices. The course addresses corporate responsibility, workplace ethics, and the broader business context in which HRD operates.
Explores ethical theories and their application to professional dilemmas across various fields. Students develop critical thinking skills for navigating complex moral issues in workplace settings.

Focuses on designing, implementing, and evaluating employee training programs. Students learn instructional design principles, needs assessment, training delivery methods, and measuring training effectiveness.
Examines how human resource development aligns with organizational strategy and business objectives. The course covers workforce planning, talent management, and using HRD as a competitive advantage.
Offers concentrated study of emerging trends, specialized issues, or current challenges in human resource development. Content varies based on industry needs and contemporary HRD research.

Teaches methods for identifying performance gaps and development needs within organizations. Students learn assessment tools and techniques for diagnosing organizational problems and recommending solutions.

Explores theories and practices for developing leadership capabilities and management skills. The course covers leadership styles, succession planning, and programs for building effective leaders at all organizational levels.

Introduces the consulting process and skills needed for internal and external HRD consulting roles. Students learn client relationship management, problem diagnosis, intervention strategies, and consulting ethics.

Studies planned change processes and interventions for improving organizational effectiveness. The course covers change management theories, resistance to change, organizational culture, and implementing sustainable transformations.

Examines individual career planning and organizational career development systems. Students explore career theories, counseling techniques, succession planning, and supporting employee career progression.

Analyzes human resource development in international and cross-cultural contexts. The course addresses global workforce challenges, expatriate training, cultural dimensions, and managing HRD across borders.

Explores emerging digital technologies and their applications in media production and communication. Students examine social media, mobile platforms, virtual reality, and how technological innovations transform media landscapes.

Develops written and oral communication skills for workplace contexts. The course covers business writing, presentations, interpersonal communication, and professional correspondence across various media, and connects said topics with AI influence and usage in todays society.

Introduces principles and techniques of visual design and artistic production for media applications. Students learn about composition, color theory, typography, and creating visual content for various platforms.
Teaches photographic techniques and visual narrative construction. Students develop skills in composition, lighting, editing, and using images to communicate stories and messages effectively.

Provides foundational knowledge of film production including pre-production, shooting, and post-production processes. Students learn basic cinematography, directing, editing, and the technical and creative aspects of filmmaking.

Examines strategies for managing organizational reputation and relationships with various publics. The course covers PR campaigns, media relations, crisis communication, and building positive public image.

Explores non-mainstream media forms including independent journalism, community media, and grassroots communication platforms. Students examine how alternative media challenges dominant narratives and serves underrepresented communities.

Studies integrated marketing communication strategies including advertising, promotions, branding, and digital marketing. The course examines how organizations create consistent messages across multiple channels to reach target audiences.

Examines the media landscape in Morocco, including press freedom, broadcasting, digital media, and journalism. The course explores the relationship between media institutions and Moroccan society, politics, and culture.

Develops critical skills for analyzing media texts, institutions, and audiences. Students learn theoretical frameworks and methodologies for examining how media produces meaning and influences society.
An intermediate course advancing students' Arabic communication proficiency. Emphasizes complex conversational scenarios and cultural nuances.

Studies communication processes within organizations including internal communication, organizational culture, and information flow. The course examines how effective communication supports organizational goals and employee engagement.
Provides focused investigation of current issues, emerging trends, or specialized areas in media studies. Course content varies to address contemporary media phenomena and research.
Offers in-depth examination of specific communication theories, contexts, or issues. Content varies to explore current developments and specialized areas within communication studies.

Builds on introductory filmmaking skills with emphasis on advanced techniques in cinematography, directing, and post-production. Students work on complex film projects and develop professional-level production capabilities.

Examines the role of communication in social and economic development processes. The course explores how media and communication strategies support development initiatives, behavior change, and community empowerment.

Focuses on creating advertising content for digital platforms including social media, websites, and mobile applications. Students learn digital design tools, copywriting, and campaign development for online environments.

Provides guided experience in planning and executing a substantial media production project. Students apply theoretical knowledge and technical skills to create professional-quality media work, often serving as a capstone experience.
Examines psychological disorders, their diagnosis, symptoms, and treatment approaches. Students learn about mental health conditions, assessment methods, and evidence-based therapeutic interventions.

Explores mental processes including perception, memory, attention, language, and problem-solving. The course examines how people acquire, process, and store information, drawing on psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence.

Studies human psychological development across the lifespan from infancy through old age. Students examine cognitive, social, emotional, and physical changes, as well as factors influencing development at different life stages.

Investigates how social contexts and group dynamics influence individual behavior and organizational functioning. The course covers topics like conformity, persuasion, group decision-making, leadership, and workplace behavior.

Examines communication patterns, relationship dynamics, and strategies for managing interpersonal conflicts. Students develop skills in negotiation, mediation, and building healthy personal and professional relationships.

Applies psychological principles to workplace issues including employee selection, performance management, motivation, and job satisfaction. The course addresses how to optimize both employee well-being and organizational productivity.

Studies how humans acquire first and second languages, examining cognitive processes, developmental stages, and factors affecting language learning. The course covers theories of language acquisition and their educational implications.

Examines psychological principles applied to teaching and learning contexts. Students explore learning theories, motivation, classroom management, assessment, and individual differences that affect educational outcomes.

Investigates psychological effects of social media use on individuals and society. The course examines topics like online identity, digital communication, social comparison, addiction, and mental health implications of social media engagement.

Analyzes psychological factors underlying political behavior, attitudes, and decision-making. Students explore topics like political identity, voting behavior, prejudice, propaganda, and the psychology of leadership and extremism.
An introductory course designed to help students transition to university life. Focuses on academic skills, time management, and campus resources.
A continuation of FYE 1101, further developing students'' academic and personal success skills. Emphasizes goal setting and university engagement.
A foundational course that builds essential academic skills for university-level work. Covers critical thinking, study strategies, and academic integrity.
An introductory writing course emphasizing critical reading and analytical writing. Students develop skills in essay composition and revision.
An advanced composition course focusing on research-based writing and argumentation. Students learn to synthesize multiple sources effectively.
A survey course exploring major works of English literature across different periods. Examines cultural and historical contexts of literary texts.
A required course for the internship, teaches students how to write and present professional written work in forms of cover letters, CVs, Technical summaries, etc.
An introductory course in Modern Standard Arabic covering basic grammar and vocabulary. Develops foundational speaking, reading, and writing skills.
A continuation of Arabic I, advancing students'' proficiency in grammar and communication. Expands vocabulary and cultural understanding.
An introductory course emphasizing practical Arabic communication skills. Develops speaking and listening abilities for everyday contexts.
A continuation of Arabic Communication I with focus on intermediate conversational skills. Enhances fluency and cultural competence with a focus on arabic usage in academic context.
This course covers the mechanics of bodies at rest.

An arabic literature course tailored towards students with a native or proficient level in arabic. This course covers concepts related to arabic poetry, texts,  essay writing, and creative writing in the arabic language.
An advanced course in French language with emphasis on french acadelic writing. Develops proficiency in reading, writing, and speaking French.
A survey of arab world history from ancient civilizations to the early modern period. Explores major political, social, and cultural developments.
A summary of World History covering ancient and modern global history. Examines imperialism, world wars, and contemporary international relations.
An introductory course to Islamic nations and societies. It compares islamic societies in the pre-islamic era and the contemporary modern era.
A survey course introducing major literary genres and critical approaches. Develops analytical skills for interpreting literary texts.
An exploration of the role of science in understanding contemporary society. Examines ethical, scientific, and cultural questions.
A study of religions from a comparative perspective across cultures. Explores universal themes and diverse religious views .
A foundational course in philosophical thinking and major philosophical questions. Explores ethics, metaphysics, and epistemology.
A systematic study of historical theories and the history behind moral reasoning. Examines contemporary ethical dilemmas and philosophical approaches.
An interdisciplinary exploration of artistic expression across islamic art pieces. Analyzes relationships between visual arts, Islamic architecture, and concluded values.

An interactive art course specifically targeting visuals such as painting, drawing, and sketching, and digital design as types of visual and interactive arts. This course combines theory and practice, focusing on practical projects.
A hands-on course introducing fundamental performing techniques and concepts. Develops creative expression through theatre and performance studies.
A discussion based course covering concepts of culture and heritage and the intersection between the two disciplines.
An introductory history course covering historical elements and principles of all various forms of arts.
An upper-level course for in-depth exploration of specialized art topics. Emphasizes critical analysis and advanced artistic practice.
A workshop course developing skills in fiction, poetry, or creative nonfiction. Emphasizes craft, revision, and peer critique.
A foundational course covering basic economic principles and theories. Examines microeconomic and macroeconomic concepts and their real-world applications.
A survey course exploring physical and human geography across the globe. Examines spatial relationships, environmental systems, and cultural landscapes.
A foundational course in psychological science covering major theories and research. Explores human behavior, cognition, and mental processes.
A comprehensive introduction to sociological perspectives and social structures. Examines social institutions, inequality, and human interaction in society.
An interdisciplinary course exploring key concepts across social science disciplines? Focusing on anthropology. Develops critical thinking about social phenomena and research methods.
A community-based learning experience connecting academic study with real-world service. Develops civic responsibility and applies classroom knowledge to community needs.
A community-based learning experience connecting academic study with real-world service. Develops civic responsibility and applies classroom knowledge to community needs.
This course is an introduction to the fundamental concepts of financial accounting.
Financial management for business and the corporation emphasizes the conceptual framework and principles of financial management for business organizations.
This course offers an overview of the art and science of management.

This course covers basic cost relationships, cost behavior, cash flow statements, financial statement analysis, including ratio analysis, horizontal, and vertical analysis cost of products for managerial decision-making, forecasting, budgeting, and profitability analysis.
This course is designed to provide foundations of statistical methods for managerial decision-making.
This course introduces concepts and methods surrounding electronic commerce practices.
This course introduces students to the role of the entrepreneur in the economic system and how to start, finance, and operate a successful business.
This course introduces the field of operations management and a state-of-the-art view of the primary activities of the operations function in manufacturing and service organizations.
This course covers the managerial and organizational issues involved in operating a firm.
This course gives an outline of common marketing concepts and models with the purpose of developing responsive marketing strategies that meet customers’ needs.
This course focuses on the use of marketing research as an aid to making marketing decisions.
This course is concerned with the development, evaluation, and implementation of marketing management in complex environments.
Supply chain management is the integration of all activities associated with the flow and transformation of goods.
This course provides an introduction to engineering design.
Introductory concepts needed to design digital systems.
This course covers the mechanics of bodies in motion.
This course covers the time value of economic resources.
The topics covered in this course include the basic principles of R-L-C circuit concepts.
This course introduces students to the properties and selection of common engineering materials used in engineering applications.
The primary goal of this course is to provide a thorough understanding and analysis of signals and systems.
The course deals with appropriate measurement techniques and proper instrumentation to acquire data.
Team-based senior design project integrating engineering knowledge from prior coursework.
In this course, the student will participate in a formal research project.
This course explores the role of the entrepreneur in the economic system.
This course introduces students to the world of microcontrollers.
This course introduces students to the fundamental principles, concepts, and characteristics of feedback control systems.
Industrial robots are widely used in industrial automation.
Calculus-based introduction to mechanics: kinematics, forces, energy, momentum, and rotation.
Electricity and magnetism, waves, and optics for science and engineering students.
Qualitative survey of motion, energy, waves, electricity, and modern physics for non-majors.
General chemistry I: atomic structure, bonding, stoichiometry, gases, and thermochemistry.
General chemistry II: kinetics, equilibria, acids/bases, thermodynamics, and electrochemistry.
Principles of ecology, ecosystems, and human impacts on the environment.
Cell structure and function, genetics, evolution, and organismal diversity.
Freshman course delving into the art of public speaking, training students to hold speeches in the professional context.
A freshman level course in academic success focusing on the principles and teachings of critical thinking in an educational context

column2: Calculus I: Differential and Integral Calculus
column3: The emphasis of this course is on problem solving, not on the presentation of theoretical considerations. While the course necessarily includes some discussion of theoretical notions, its primary objective is not the production of theorem-provers. The syllabus for MTH 1303 includes most of the elementary topics in the theory of real-valued functions of a real variable: limits, continuity, derivatives, maxima and minima, integration, trigonometric, logarithmic, and exponential functions and techniques of integration.
This course covers the fundamentals of converting energy, thermodynamic properties of liquids and gases.
This course covers basic principles of fluid statics and dynamics.
This course consists of on-the-job education and training in a public or private sector agency or business related to the student's field.
Sophomore course that focuses on fundamental mechanics knowledge to better understand materials

This course introduces students to mathematical methods for making optimal decisions in complex systems. Students should expect to learn techniques for modeling real-world problems and finding the best solutions under constraints.

This course introduces students to random processes that evolve over time, providing tools to model and analyze systems with inherent uncertainty and randomness. Students should expect to move beyond basic probability and statistics to study dynamic systems where outcomes are probabilistic rather than deterministic.
This course teaches students the basics of project management, including but not limited to project planning and scheduling, resource management and budgeting, and risk management.

This course explores how organizations use information technology and systems to achieve business objectives, improve decision-making, and gain competitive advantages. Students should expect to understand the intersection of business strategy, technology, and organizational processes.

This course provides students with foundational statistical methods essential for analyzing data and making informed engineering decisions under uncertainty. Students should expect to learn how to collect, analyze, and interpret data to solve practical engineering problems.

This course focuses on how organizations design, manage, and improve the processes that create goods and services. Students should expect to learn systematic approaches to making operations more efficient, cost-effective, and responsive to customer needs.

The course is designed for early exposure and understanding of the practical and
theoretical in supply chain management and sustainability to the students. It guides
students to develop an effective SCM strategy and its activities, as well as understand
the relationships that exist among a chain of firms that work together to provide a
product or service. It shall cover the quality followings: supply chain strategy, sourcing
strategy, logistic management, distribution management, production and inventory
management, measuring supply chain performance, information technology in supply
chain, coordination in supply chain, and sustainability. The learning process for this
course will be conducted through lectures, case studies practices, discussion, group
project, and presentation.

This course studies the processes involved in the planning and coordination of
delivering persons or goods from one origin to a destination. Students learn to master
transportation management system (TMS) and other strategic business tools for an
effective control of transportation cost management. The course targets among other
learning outcomes, solving for the variants of vehicle routing problems as an effective
way for fleet management.

This course introduces the quality management principles and the role of total quality
in all key economic sectors. It also gives an overview of the philosophical perspectives
supporting total quality. Finally, it provides basic technical tools and techniquesrelevant
to quality assurance, control, and improvement, including management
297
models such as the Deming Cycle, Six Sigma programs, and the seven Quality Control
tools.

A practical course on analyzing data that arise sequentially in time (e.g., sales volume,
precipitation, GDP, demand, unemployment rates, etc.). The course will teach
students: how to detect trends and underlying seasonal patterns; how to use the BoxJenkins methodology, autoregressive, and moving average processes; and about
exponential smoothing, classical decomposition, and regression methods. It will also
257
provide an introduction to multivariate time series and Neural Networks Autoregression.

This course is aimed at equipping students with the knowledge on discrete-event
simulation. A software will be used to model, build, and run simulation models. The
course covers topics on discrete-event approaches, representing uncertainty, tracedriven simulation, input data analytics, modelling and building simulation models,
verifying and validating simulation models, experimentation and running of simulation
models, analysis of output results, etc. Promodel/Awsim for Facility Design; Auto CAD
for Product design; and R-Studio/SPSS for Statistical Analysis.

This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamentals of nonlinear
optimization and their applications in engineering. The course will cover both
unconstrained and constrained optimization, convex and non-convex optimization, as
well as algorithms and software tools commonly used in nonlinear optimization.
Students will also learn about real-world applications of nonlinear optimization in
various engineering fields

This course is designed for SSE students who have decided to undergo a thematic

area in Biotechnology. The course is a continuity to BIO 1401 with more depth in the
cellular and molecular aspects that govern the organization and function of living
organisms.
In this course, students will cover and understand the major mechanisms that relate
the structure to the function of living organisms. Gene expression, gene regulation,
protein production, cell signaling, as well as cellular secretion mechanisms. The basics
microbiology and molecular immunology will also be addressed in this course.

This course introduces the field of biotechnology with a broad view. Students will learn
the processes and methods used to manipulate living organisms and products from
these organisms for medical, agricultural, and industrial purposes. The course will
cover the wide spectrum of molecular biotechnology, gene expression, protein
purification and basic functional genomics, and will shed light on their application in

column2: Techniques and Regulations in Applied Biotechnology
column3:
This course focuses on applied biotechnology with a focus on medicine, agriculture
and applied research. The course will be combined of lectures and a series of seminars
addressed by specialists from diverse disciplines and specialties that relate to
biotechnology. The course will cover most popular biotech techniques (advanced
genome sequencing, flow cytometry, cell transfection, molecular labelling, etc.) as well
as the regulations in different fields of biotechnology, with an emphasis on biosafety,

This is an overview of general monetary and banking policies. It deals with the supply
of money for a nation and the relationship of commercial banking with the supply and
demand for money. This course also analyses monetary concepts, central banking
functions, and techniques of monetary stabilization.

This course continues the study of financial decision-making in corporations. The main
topics covered are advanced ratios analysis, capital budgeting, capital structure,
dividend policy, and an introduction to portfolio management. The course also provides
an in-depth analysis of financial problems with the organization, operation, merger, and
dissolution of corporations.

This course introduces students to the world of international finance, investment, and
business. Standard financial management and the multidimensional world of decisionmaking within a global context are addressed.

This course cannot be taken abroad or on exchange. This course focuses on the organization and operation of both American and Moroccan
legal systems, legal rules, and ethical constraints that impact business, and the
practical application of these rules and constraints to real-world situations. Emphasis
is placed on analytical problem solving and ethical decision-making.

This course introduces students to power electronics and explains the applications of
solid-state electronics for the control and conversion of electric power. The course
covers the main power electronics topics - namely, power computations, dc-dc
converters, dc power supplies, inverters, rectifiers, and drive and snubber circuits.

This course covers the following topics: Strength of material, Aircraft Structural Detail;
Structural Idealization, Aircraft materials, Loads on Aircraft Structures, Shear forces,
Moments, Bending and Twisting in Aircraft structural components, Theory of Elasticity,
Bending and Twisting of thin-walled cross-sections, Shearing in thin-walled beams,
236 and Force Analysis in Landing Gears.

This course provides students with required basic air flow laws, potential flow theory,
airfoil theory, finite wing theory as well as linearized supersonic flow. It covers the
following topics: Two-Dimensional Inviscid Fluid Flow; Stream Function and Velocity
Potential; Superposition of Elementary Flows; Thin Airfoil Theory; Finite Wings;
Incompressible Boundary Layer; Oblique shock waves and expansion waves; and
Airfoils in supersonic flow.

This course covers topics selected from the disciplines of fluid mechanics, engineering
thermodynamics, heat transfer, and combustion to study energy systems, aircraft
propulsion, etc. This course prepares students for advanced analysis of energy
systems and propulsion’s system components. Students completing this course should
be able to perform thermodynamic analysis for thermophysical problems in energy
systems involving heat transfer and combustion.

This course provides students with the necessary knowledge to understand, define,
and calculate different aeronautical vehicle performance configurations. It covers the
following topics: Aircraft performance in steady flight; Straight and level flight; Flight
limitations; Drag; performance curves in terms of thrust and power; Gliding flight;
Range and endurance; Climbing flight; Aircraft performance in accelerated flight; Takeoff and landing; and Turning flight.
